passage: Rafiq sits across from me at the consulting firm, so I have watched him for two years. On client calls his English is polished, precise, slightly formal. Ten minutes later he is on the phone with his mother, and it's Dakhni with a loud laugh that makes the whole row smile. He keeps a small notebook of Dakhni proverbs from his mother and reads one to his nephew on video every Sunday. I can't say for sure whether he ever feels fake when he switches. He doesn't look it; he looks like a man using the right tool for the right job. Once I asked him. He said, "The English gets me work. The Dakhni keeps me whole." Anand

qa.a: Probably happy and close, since his Dakhni keeps them connected.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage: Monday. In his first week at a Bengaluru software firm, Harish rehearsed every sentence in polished English and felt like a fraud. That evening he spoke Kannada with his mother on the phone and relaxed at once, and felt guilty about the difference. Wednesday. His senior colleague Pradeep, hearing him practise, said, "You're not being fake. You're switching tools. My grandmother's Tulu and my client English are both mine." Harish laughed, surprised. Saturday. Harish ran a client call in clear English without rehearsing. Afterwards he taught his cousin a Kannada tongue-twister on video and laughed until he coughed. He felt like the same person both times.

qa.q: What did Pradeep say about switching?
qa.a: Pradeep said, "You're not being fake. You're switching tools."

qa.q: How did Harish feel on Monday about his rehearsed English?
qa.a: Harish felt like a fraud and a little guilty about how different he sounded at home.

qa.q: What turning point on Wednesday changed how Harish saw his two ways of speaking?
qa.a: Pradeep told him it was switching tools, not being fake, and gave his own example of Tulu and client English, so Harish stopped seeing one as false.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Harish's worry?
qa.a: As familiar, since Pradeep also moves between a grandmother's Tulu and client English and calls both his own.

grounding: A young adult moves between casual home speech and polished professional English without feeling fake and sees each register as a tool.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
Varun, you told me today you feel "fake" in client meetings. Let Eshaan Sir tell you something from twenty years ago.
I was twenty-four, my first job at a bank in Mumbai. At home in Kanpur we spoke Awadhi-Hindi. In the office, everyone spoke polished English, and I practised mine in the mirror every night.
One day, my manager heard me on the phone with my mother, speaking Awadhi. I blushed. He said, "Two languages, two tools. Don't throw either away."
I thought about that. After that, I stopped apologising for my accent. At client meetings, I used my best English. At lunch with the peons and drivers, I spoke Hindi. With my mother, Awadhi. I felt whole, not fake, because I never pretended the other parts didn't exist.
So, Varun, use your English for the clients. And call your grandmother in Bhojpuri tonight.

qa.q: What did Eshaan practise in the mirror every night?
qa.a: He practised his English in the mirror every night.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when the manager heard him speak Awadhi?
qa.a: Eshaan felt embarrassed, blushing at being overheard speaking his home language.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Eshaan's story?
qa.a: The manager's words about two languages being two tools helped Eshaan stop apologising and use each language where it fit.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's mother have felt hearing him keep Awadhi?
qa.a: She would probably feel close to him and reassured that city life hadn't taken away their shared language.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls learning to move between polished English at work and his mother tongue at home without feeling fake.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
The client call from Singapore was starting in three minutes, and Keerthana's phone buzzed. Amma. She picked up.
"Kanna, did you eat? Appa's medicine came?" in fast Tamil.
"Saaptaen, Amma. I'll call after the meeting, okay?" Keerthana answered, laughing, in the same Tamil.
Sachin, her teammate, was setting up the screen. When she hung up, he grinned. "Two minutes later you'll sound like a newsreader."
The call began. Keerthana, twenty-five, switched into crisp, polished English, walking the client through the numbers without a single slip.
Afterwards, Sachin said, "Doesn't it feel weird? Like two people?"
Keerthana thought about it. "No. It's one person with two toolkits. Tamil is where I rest. English is where I work." She picked up her phone. "Now I'm calling Amma back."

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the client call when Amma called?
qa.a: The call from Singapore was starting in three minutes.

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel about switching between Tamil and English?
qa.a: Keerthana feels comfortable and whole, not fake; she sees herself as one person with two toolkits.

qa.q: What does Keerthana's approach show others?
qa.a: Each language is a tool: polished English serves work, while keeping Tamil with Amma keeps her rooted.

qa.q: How does Sachin seem to see Keerthana's switching?
qa.a: Sachin is amused and curious, wondering if it feels like being two people.

grounding: Right before a client call, a young adult moves from casual Tamil with her mother to polished English at work without feeling fake.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
In the open-plan office in Andheri, Shreya, twenty-four, had just finished presenting to the regional heads in careful, polished English. Her colleague Pranav leaned over. "Where did that accent come from? At lunch you sound like a Dadar fish market."
A few people laughed. Shreya felt a flicker of irritation, then let it go.
"At lunch I speak Marathi, because that's who I am," she said. "In meetings I speak English, because that's my job. Both are me."
Pranav raised his eyebrows. "Isn't it tiring?"
"Less tiring than pretending I'm only one of them."
That evening, on the local train, she called her Aai in Marathi and laughed about the presentation. Then she replied to a work email in English, and switched back again mid-sentence to tell Aai about the dinner she wanted.

qa.q: Where was the open-plan office?
qa.a: The open-plan office was in Andheri.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when people laughed at Pranav's remark?
qa.a: Shreya felt a flicker of irritation, but she stayed calm and let it go.

qa.q: Why is Shreya's answer to Pranav a wise one?
qa.a: She explains that each language suits a place, work English and home Marathi, and that using both keeps her whole rather than fake.

qa.q: How might Pranav see code-switching after Shreya's reply?
qa.a: Pranav may begin to see switching languages as a skill, not a fake accent, since Shreya explains it simply.

grounding: A young adult moves between polished professional English and her mother tongue without feeling fake, keeping both parts of herself alive.

passage:
"...so we'll share the revised timeline by Thursday, end of day. Thank you, Martin." Lalit clicked off the call.
His phone buzzed. "Haan, Maa. Khana kha liya. Arre, tension mat lo, chhata le ke gaya tha."
Asif looked up from the next desk, grinning. "Two different people in one minute."
"Same person, two tools," Lalit said. "Martin needs the tidy English. Maa needs me."
"Doesn't it feel fake? I feel fake in meetings sometimes."
"I used to. Then I noticed I don't feel fake speaking Hindi to my Nani and Marwari to my Dadi. Why should English be different?"
"Marwari too?"
"Only with Dadi. If I stop, it goes out of our house."
Asif leaned back. "My Ammi keeps telling me to speak Urdu with my niece."
"Then do it," Lalit said, already typing the timeline email.

qa.q: By when did Lalit promise the revised timeline?
qa.a: By Thursday, end of day.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel about switching between English and home languages?
qa.a: Lalit feels comfortable and whole, not fake, seeing each language as a tool for a different person.

qa.q: What could Asif take from Lalit's approach?
qa.a: Asif could treat meeting English as one tool rather than a mask, and keep Urdu alive by speaking it with the niece as Ammi suggests.

qa.q: Why might Asif feel fake in meetings when Lalit does not?
qa.a: Asif may still see polished English as a different self rather than a register, so switching feels like hiding instead of choosing a tool.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who moves between polished work English and home languages without feeling fake, and keeps a family language alive.
